headline.headline: RAYS CLAW BACK FROM THE BRINK, STUN BREWERS IN 12 TO FORCE GAME 5
headline.deck: Tampa Bay scores twice in the 12th inning to deny Milwaukee its first championship
headline.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Milwaukee Brewers were three outs from history Tuesday night, clinging to a 3-2 lead in the bottom of the 12th inning of Game 4 of the World Series. Then the Tampa Bay Rays reminded 40,514 fans at Tropicana Field, and everyone watching across the country, why October refuses to follow a script. The Rays pushed across two runs in the 12th to win 4-3, sending the Series back to Milwaukee for a Game 5 on Wednesday night.

The game was a pitchers' duel for most of its grinding four hours and 20 minutes. Tampa Bay scratched out a run in the second inning and Milwaukee answered with one in the fourth. The Brewers took the lead in the fifth and held it through nine innings of regulation, then through extra frames that stretched the tension to its absolute limit. Neither club scored again until the 12th, when the Rays finally broke through against a Brewers bullpen that had nothing left to give. Jax earned the win in relief, the pivotal decision of the night.

For Milwaukee, the collapse in the 12th will sting for days. The Brewers had executed a near-perfect game plan, limiting Tampa Bay's offense to a trickle for nearly 11 full innings. But the Rays' resilience, the very trait that has defined this franchise through decades of small-market baseball, surfaced at the worst possible moment for Milwaukee. The World Series, which looked headed for a four-game sweep just hours ago, now belongs entirely to Game 5.

secondary.headline: CELTICS SURVIVE NETS IN OVERTIME THRILLER, 125-124
secondary.deck: Boston escapes Brooklyn by a single point to advance in Eastern Conference semifinals
secondary.body:
BOSTON — One point. After four quarters and one overtime period, that was all that separated the Boston Celtics from the Brooklyn Nets on Tuesday night at TD Garden. The Celtics held on for a 125-124 victory in what amounted to one of the tightest games of the second round, keeping their Eastern Conference semifinal hopes very much alive.

Elsewhere in the Eastern Conference, the New York Knicks handled the Detroit Pistons with far less drama, rolling to a 111-97 victory. The Knicks controlled that game throughout, a welcome result for a franchise that has been grinding through a difficult stretch in recent weeks. In the Western Conference, the San Antonio Spurs were dominant, dismantling the Sacramento Kings 130-103 in a performance that served notice to the rest of the bracket.

secondary.headline: MORANT AND LILLARD TORCH LAKERS AS PORTLAND STAYS PERFECT
secondary.deck: Trail Blazers remain unbeaten despite Doncic dropping 41 points in a losing effort
secondary.body:
PORTLAND, Ore. — Luka Doncic scored 41 points and it still was not enough. Ja Morant and Deni Avdija each finished with 23 points, Damian Lillard added 21 and buried a clutch three-pointer with 43 seconds remaining, and the Portland Trail Blazers remained unbeaten with a 136-129 victory over the Los Angeles Lakers on Tuesday night. Portland, fourth in the Western Conference, improved to 2-0 and showed it can absorb a star's best performance and still find a way to win.

The Blazers' formula was straightforward and devastating. Morant attacked the paint relentlessly while Lillard provided the outside shooting that opened the floor. Avdija was a consistent third option throughout. Doncic's night was a marvel in defeat, a reminder that Los Angeles has a weapon capable of taking over any game, but the Lakers' supporting cast could not keep pace with Portland's three-headed offensive attack. The Trail Blazers now await Memphis, which is seeking its fourth straight road win and arrives carrying a 4-0 record.

secondary.headline: COLTS DEAL BUCKNER, NELSON IN SIGNAL OF FULL REBUILD
secondary.deck: Indianapolis ships two franchise cornerstones to contenders, raising questions about Jonathan Taylor
secondary.body:
INDIANAPOLIS — The Indianapolis Colts did not move one cornerstone this week. They moved two. Defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and offensive guard Quenton Nelson were dealt to contending teams Tuesday in a pair of trades that announced, loudly and clearly, that Indianapolis is tearing things down and starting over. Buckner heads to San Francisco, where the 49ers believe he can push them back into Super Bowl contention. Nelson lands in Seattle, where the Seahawks are betting the veteran guard can shore up an offensive line in need of an upgrade.

The trades immediately raised the question that the rest of the league is already asking: is running back Jonathan Taylor next? Taylor remains one of the most talented backs in football, and a rebuilding Colts team has every incentive to collect additional draft capital. Green Bay edge rusher Micah Parsons, meanwhile, may be nearing a return to practice after more than 10 months away from the field, according to coach Matt LaFleur, adding another layer of intrigue to an offseason that has already reshaped multiple rosters.

column.headline: MILWAUKEE HAD ITS MOMENT. THE RAYS STOLE IT BACK.
column.body:
There is a particular cruelty in being three outs away. Not three innings. Not three games. Three outs from the first World Series title in Milwaukee Brewers history, and the Rays reached into the 12th inning and took it all back. Tuesday night at Tropicana Field was not merely a baseball game. It was a reminder that no lead in October is safe until the final out is recorded, and that Tampa Bay, perennially outspent and underestimated, has an institutional memory of suffering that transforms into genuine resilience when the stakes are highest.

The Brewers now face the most dangerous game in baseball: a Game 5 on their home field with the weight of a lost sweep pressing down on the dugout. History says the team that blows a chance to close out a series on the road frequently pays for it. Milwaukee has the pitching and the crowd. Tampa Bay has momentum, Jax on the mound, and the particular confidence of a club that just refused to die. Game 5 may well be the best baseball of the entire October. That is the gift the Rays gave the sport Tuesday night, even if Milwaukee is not yet in a mood to appreciate it.

story.headline: RAYS STORM BACK IN 12TH TO STAY ALIVE, FORCE WORLD SERIES GAME 5
story.deck: Tampa Bay scores twice in final frame to deny Brewers' sweep bid
story.body:
TAMPA, Fla. -- Milwaukee was three outs from its first World Series championship. Instead, the Tampa Bay Rays pushed across two runs in the bottom of the 12th inning Tuesday night at Tropicana Field to defeat the Brewers 4-3, forcing a Game 5 and denying Milwaukee what would have been the 22nd sweep in Fall Classic history. Winning pitcher Jax earned the decision in the marathon affair, which consumed four hours and 20 minutes in front of 40,514 spectators.

The Rays trailed 3-2 entering the 12th after Milwaukee plated a run in both the fourth and fifth innings and Tampa Bay answered with single tallies in the second and fourth. The game sat deadlocked through six consecutive scoreless innings from the fifth through the 11th before the Rays finally cracked the tie. A pinch-hit single by an unidentified batter for Mesa Jr. ignited the rally, and with courtesy runners deployed for both Caminero and Hicks L., Tampa Bay pushed across the decisive pair of runs to complete the comeback.

Home runs by Pratt, his first of the series, and Hamilton, his second, supplied the early offensive backbone for both clubs. Christian Yelich added a stolen base for Milwaukee, which stranded 10 runners and could not deliver the knockout blow despite multiple opportunities. Aaron Ashby had already set a postseason record for scoreless innings by a reliever earlier in the series. Game 5 is scheduled for Wednesday night, with the Brewers still holding a 3-1 series advantage.

story.headline: MORANT, LILLARD GUN DOWN LAKERS AS BLAZERS SURVIVE DONCIC'S 41-POINT BARRAGE
story.deck: Portland stays unbeaten at 2-0 despite Doncic's heroics in a seven-point thriller
story.body:
LOS ANGELES — Ja Morant and Damian Lillard would not let Luka Doncic beat them. Morant and Deni Avdija each poured in 23 points, Lillard added 21 and drilled a clutch three-pointer with 43 seconds remaining as the Portland Trail Blazers held off the Los Angeles Lakers 136-129 Tuesday night at Crypto.com Arena, improving to 2-0 on the young season despite a 41-point performance from Doncic that kept the Lakers within striking distance throughout.

The Blazers' three-headed backcourt attack proved too much for Los Angeles to contain. Lillard's late three-pointer, his most critical shot of the night, effectively iced a game that the Lakers refused to concede. Doncic was relentless, shouldering the offensive load for a Lakers squad that could not manufacture enough complementary scoring to close the gap against a Portland team playing with the kind of cohesion that has the Western Conference taking notice.

Elsewhere around the league Tuesday, the Boston Celtics survived Brooklyn in overtime, 125-124, in the night's tightest finish. The New York Knicks handled the Detroit Pistons 111-97 at Madison Square Garden, and the San Antonio Spurs rolled past the Sacramento Kings 130-103 at home. Portland now awaits the Memphis Grizzlies, who arrive riding a four-game winning streak and carry a 4-0 record into Wednesday night's Western Conference showdown.

boxScores.title: Portland Trail Blazers 136, Los Angeles Lakers 129

story.headline: DEVILS RIDE HISCHIER'S HOT HAND INTO DENVER SHOWDOWN
story.deck: New Jersey star netted twice as Devils carry momentum into Colorado clash.
story.body:
Nico Hischier buried two goals in New Jersey's latest victory, and the Devils carry that momentum into Denver Wednesday night when they face the Colorado Avalanche at Ball Arena. New Jersey enters the matchup at 8-4, among the sturdiest records in the Metropolitan Division, while Colorado sits at 6-5-1 and badly needs a result on home ice against a Devils squad that has been one of the Eastern Conference's most dangerous teams through the young season.

Hischier's two-goal performance gives him a spotlight heading into a marquee Central Division venue, and the Devils will look to exploit any defensive cracks in an Avalanche group still searching for consistency. Colorado's 6-5-1 mark reflects a team capable of stretching any opponent but prone to giving up points it cannot afford in a crowded Central Division race.

Elsewhere around the league Wednesday, the Montreal Canadiens bring a three-game winning streak and a sharp 7-3-2 record into Dallas to face the Stars, setting up one of the night's most competitive matchups. In Anaheim, the Ducks host Buffalo's JJ Greer, who is riding a two-goal game, while Detroit squares off against Chicago and Vancouver visits San Jose following the Canucks' recent shootout triumph.

story.headline: QUARTERBACK CAROUSEL SPINS WILD AS TEAMS RESHAPE ROSTERS FOR 2026
story.deck: Three teams swap signal-callers in a frenzied May that has scouts scrambling.
story.body:
The NFL offseason took another dramatic turn this week as the Las Vegas Raiders agreed to terms with veteran quarterback Sam Darnold on a two-year, $58 million contract, signaling the franchise's latest attempt to stabilize a position that has churned through seven starters in eight seasons. Darnold, who led the Minnesota Vikings to the NFC Championship Game in 2025 before Minnesota pivoted to draft a successor, brings a proven if streaky résumé to a Raiders offense that finished 28th in scoring last season. General manager Tom Telesco called the signing a bridge to the future, a phrase that has earned considerable skepticism in Silver and Black territory.

Meanwhile, the Carolina Panthers pulled off the offseason's most surprising trade, sending disgruntled wide receiver Jonathan Mingo and a 2027 second-round pick to the Denver Broncos in exchange for cornerback Pat Surtain III, son of the legendary Pat Surtain II. Carolina's secondary ranked dead last in passing yards allowed in 2025, and head coach Dave Canales made no secret of his desire to add an elite cover man before training camp opens in late July. Broncos brass, rebuilding around their own young core, welcomed the additional draft capital as they continue to construct depth behind a promising but unproven offensive line.

On the draft analysis front, three weeks removed from the 2026 NFL Draft, early reviews of the first-round class are beginning to crystallize among league insiders. Tennessee Titans offensive tackle Marcus Webb, the fifth overall pick out of Georgia, has already drawn raves from the Titans coaching staff during voluntary OTAs, with position coach Jim Donahue comparing Webb's footwork to a young Trent Williams. The New York Giants, who traded up to select Ohio State linebacker Darius Coleman at 11, saw their stock rise further when Coleman posted a sub-4.4 time in informal workouts last week, quieting critics who questioned his burst against NFL-caliber speed.
